reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / Shields' Textbook of Glaucoma
clinicalPearls: A secondary glaucoma arising in eyes with intraocular inflammation, with pressure elevation resulting from several coexisting mechanisms rather than a single cause
Open-angle mechanisms include trabecular obstruction by inflammatory cells and debris, trabeculitis, and a steroid-induced pressure response from treatment
Angle-closure mechanisms include pupillary block from extensive posterior synechiae with iris bombe, and peripheral anterior synechiae from chronic angle inflammation
Pressure may paradoxically be low during active inflammation from ciliary hyposecretion, then surge as inflammation settles or steroids are used
Careful gonioscopy is essential to distinguish open-angle from synechial or pupillary-block mechanisms because treatment differs

Management balances vigorous control of inflammation with pressure-lowering therapy, while recognising that corticosteroids can both reduce inflammatory outflow obstruction and independently raise pressure
Fuchs heterochromic uveitis and herpetic anterior uveitis are characteristically associated with raised pressure
Prostaglandin analogues are used with caution as they may theoretically aggravate inflammation and cystoid macular oedema
reference.pathophysiology: In uveitic glaucoma intraocular inflammation raises pressure through multiple overlapping pathways. Inflammatory cells, fibrin, and protein clog the trabecular meshwork, and direct inflammation of the meshwork (trabeculitis) reduces outflow facility; scarring can permanently damage the drainage tissue. Chronic inflammation promotes peripheral anterior synechiae that close the angle, while dense posterior synechiae binding the pupil margin to the lens can produce pupillary block with forward bowing of the iris (iris bombe) and secondary angle closure. Corticosteroids used to treat the uveitis may themselves reduce outflow and cause a steroid-induced pressure rise. Active inflammation can transiently lower pressure by suppressing aqueous production, masking a tendency to later elevation.
additionalDifferentials: Primary open-angle glaucoma with coincidental uveitis
Primary or secondary angle-closure glaucoma from other causes
Herpetic or Fuchs heterochromic uveitis with raised pressure
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination to grade inflammation, keratic precipitates, and synechiae
Gonioscopy to identify open-angle, synechial, or pupillary-block mechanisms
Applanation tonometry with monitoring during and after inflammatory episodes and steroid treatment
OCT of the optic nerve and macula to assess glaucomatous damage and cystoid oedema
Automated perimetry to monitor field loss
Targeted workup for the underlying uveitis, including infective and systemic causes when indicated
redFlags: Iris bombe from a completely bound-down pupil producing acute pupillary-block angle closure
A marked steroid-induced pressure rise during treatment of the inflammation
Very high pressure with corneal oedema during an inflammatory crisis
Progressive optic-nerve damage masked by intermittently low pressure during active uveitis
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on controlling the underlying inflammation and the mechanism of pressure rise; open-angle inflammatory hypertension often resolves as the uveitis settles, whereas extensive synechial closure and repeated crises lead to chronic glaucoma that may need drainage surgery and carries a guarded outlook.
pitfalls: Attributing all pressure elevation to steroid response and undertreating the inflammation, or vice versa
Missing pupillary block and iris bombe requiring urgent iridotomy rather than only medical therapy
Being reassured by low pressure during active inflammation and overlooking later surges
Using prostaglandin analogues uncritically where they may worsen inflammation or macular oedema
Failing to investigate and treat the underlying cause of the uveitis
